claim: CDMD is a method for automated refinement of atomistic models into cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) maps at resolutions ranging from near-atomic to subnanometer.
source: We present a correlation-driven molecular dynamics (CDMD) method for automated refinement of atomistic models into cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) maps at resolutions ranging from near-atomic to subnanometer.
evidence: The abstract directly states the method and its capabilities.

claim: CDMD utilizes a chemically accurate force field and thermodynamic sampling to improve the real-space correlation between the modeled structure and the cryo-EM map.
source: It utilizes a chemically accurate force field and thermodynamic sampling to improve the real-space correlation between the modeled structure and the cryo-EM map.
evidence: The abstract describes the technical approach of the method.

claim: CDMD employs a gradual increase in resolution and map-model agreement as well as simulated annealing.
source: Our framework employs a gradual increase in resolution and map-model agreement as well as simulated annealing, and allows fully automated refinement without manual intervention or any additional rotamer- and backbone-specific restraints.
evidence: The abstract describes the protocol features.

claim: CDMD allows fully automated refinement without manual intervention or any additional rotamer- and backbone-specific restraints.
source: Our framework employs a gradual increase in resolution and map-model agreement as well as simulated annealing, and allows fully automated refinement without manual intervention or any additional rotamer- and backbone-specific restraints.
evidence: The abstract states the automation capability.

claim: CDMD performs best in most cases compared to several well-established methods.
source: To provide an objective comparison, we apply several well-established methods across all examples and demonstrate that CDMD performs best in most cases.
evidence: The abstract summarizes the comparative results.

claim: State-of-the-art cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) allows biomolecules to be resolved in different functional states and at near-atomic resolution previously achieved only by X-ray crystallography.
source: State-of-the-art cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) allows biomolecules to be resolved in different functional states and at near-atomic resolution previously achieved only by X-ray crystallography (Zhang and Nogales, 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this claim about cryo-EM capabilities.

claim: A new generation of electron detectors and the development of sample motion correction algorithms have been the major contributors to rapid progress in cryo-EM.
source: A new generation of electron detectors and the development of sample motion correction algorithms have been the major contributors to this rapid progress (Bai et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this claim about technological advances.

claim: Cryo-EM maps determined to resolutions better than 4 Å have become standard with several examples claimed to break the 2Å-resolution barrier.
source: Cryo-EM maps determined to resolutions better than 4 Å have become standard with several examples claimed to break the 2Å-resolution barrier (Frank, 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this claim about resolution achievements.

claim: Methods for deriving accurate atomistic models from cryo-EM maps lag behind the resolution revolution.
source: However, methods for deriving accurate atomistic models from cryo-EM maps lag behind this resolution revolution (Saibil, 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this claim about the gap in methodology.

claim: Many methods are available for de novo building of polypeptide/nucleotide chains.
source: For de novo building of polypeptide/nucleotide chains many methods are available (Emsley and Cowtan, 2004; Langer et al., 2008; Terwilliger et al., 2008; Adams et al., 2010; Burnley et al., 2017), including tools for subsequent refinement of hand-built or homology models into densities (Chen et al., 2003; Fabiola and Chapman, 2005; Schröder et al., 2007; Topf et al., 2008; Brown et al., 2015; Lopéz-Blanco and Chacón, 2013; Wu et al., 2013; DiMaio et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016a; Kovalevskiy et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple references to support this claim about available methods.

claim: In non-MD refinement methods, stereochemical properties and local electrostatics are not fully enforced, nor is a proper description of large-scale concerted motions guaranteed.
source: In these methods, stereochemical properties and local electrostatics are not fully enforced, nor is a proper description of large-scale concerted motions guaranteed.
evidence: The introduction describes limitations of existing methods.

claim: When applied to maps with medium (local) resolutions or lower, non-MD methods tend to produce errors such as atomic clashes, improper bond lengths and angles, and poor agreement between the density and the corresponding model.
source: When applied to maps with medium (local) resolutions or lower, they tend to produce errors such as atomic clashes, improper bond lengths and angles, and poor agreement between the density and the corresponding model (Hooft et al., 1996; Neumann et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites references to support this claim about errors in existing methods.

claim: Multiple rotamer, backbone and secondary structure restraints, manual intervention on the system during refinement, and subsequent re-refinement are often required to preserve stereochemical plausibility and avoid overfitting.
source: As a result, multiple rotamer, backbone and secondary structure restraints, manual intervention on the system during refinement, and subsequent re-refinement are often required to preserve stereochemical plausibility and avoid overfitting.
evidence: The introduction describes the requirements of existing methods.

claim: Several molecular dynamics (MD)-based refinement methods have been developed.
source: As an alternative, several molecular dynamics (MD)-based refinement methods have been developed (Brünger et al., 1987; Brunger and Adams, 2002; Trabuco et al., 2008; Orzechowski and Tama, 2008; Fenn et al., 2011; McGreevy et al., 2016; Miyashita et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple references to support this claim about MD-based methods.

claim: MD-based refinement rests on a chemically accurate force field and thermodynamic sampling of conformations in addition to guiding the model into the density.
source: Here, the refinement rests on a chemically accurate force field and thermodynamic sampling of conformations in addition to guiding the model into the density, as opposed to minimizing a simple target function.
evidence: The introduction describes the approach of MD-based methods.

claim: MD-based methods have markedly higher computational requirements which are usually met by today's efficient parallel and GPU implementations.
source: These MD-based methods have markedly higher computational requirements which are usually met by today's efficient parallel and GPU implementations.
evidence: The introduction describes the computational requirements of MD-based methods.

claim: High-resolution maps pose a challenge to MD-based refinement.
source: High-resolution maps, however, pose a challenge to MD-based refinement (McGreevy et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this claim about challenges in MD-based refinement.

claim: Parts of the system get trapped due to inefficient conformational sampling in rugged density regions commonly present in high-resolution maps.
source: Frequently, parts of the system get trapped due to inefficient conformational sampling in rugged density regions commonly present in such maps.
evidence: The introduction describes a specific challenge in MD-based refinement.

claim: The obtained models from MD-based refinement still strongly depend on local map resolution and the choice of a particular refinement scheme or force field.
source: Despite recent improvements (McGreevy et al., 2016; Miyashita et al., 2017), the obtained models still strongly depend on local map resolution and the choice of a particular refinement scheme or force field.
evidence: The introduction cites references to support this claim about dependencies in MD-based refinement.

claim: Systematic, force-field driven deviations in model geometry have been reported.
source: Also, systematic, force-field driven deviations in model geometry have been reported (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this claim about force field issues.

claim: No available cryo-EM refinement method simultaneously meets the three challenges posed by the current resolution revolution: resolution-independent density fitting, stereochemical accuracy, and automation.
source: It is therefore fair to say that no available cryo-EM refinement method simultaneously meets the three challenges posed by the current resolution revolution: resolution-independent density fitting, stereochemical accuracy, and automation.
evidence: The introduction summarizes the state of the field.

claim: CDMD combines a previously published methodology for low-resolution maps with continuously adaptive resolution and simulated annealing.
source: Here, we have developed and implemented such an automated yet accurate method for structure refinement and validation, denoted correlation-driven molecular dynamics (CDMD), by combining a previously published methodology for low-resolution maps (Orzechowski and Tama, 2008) with continuously adaptive resolution and simulated annealing (Brünger et al., 1987; Brunger and Adams, 2002).
evidence: The introduction describes the development of CDMD with citations.

claim: CDMD was challenged to refine distant starting models of diverse quality against cryo-EM densities at various resolutions (2.6–7 Å).
source: In all the presented application examples, we challenge CDMD to refine distant starting models of diverse quality against cryo-EM densities at various resolutions (2.6–7 Å).
evidence: The introduction describes the test cases used.

claim: Performance of CDMD is assessed using commonly defined measures such as the radius of convergence, model geometry and overfitting.
source: Performance is assessed using commonly defined measures such as the radius of convergence, model geometry and overfitting.
evidence: The introduction describes the assessment criteria.

claim: Only the simulated density is continuously resampled so that the full experimental density is used throughout the refinement.
source: In contrast to previous approaches (Singharoy et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018), only the simulated density is continuously resampled so that the full experimental density is used throughout the refinement.
evidence: The Results section describes a difference from previous approaches with citations.

claim: Higher force constants at late refinement stages are required to ensure an accurate density fit at the side chain level for high-resolution maps.
source: For high-resolution maps, higher force constants at late refinement stages are required to ensure an accurate density fit at the side chain level which could otherwise be distorted by thermal fluctuations.
evidence: The Results section explains the need for higher force constants.

claim: High-temperature simulated annealing is used to enhance local map-model agreement (e.g. side chain rotamers), while keeping well-refined parts of the model unchanged.
source: Third, high-temperature simulated annealing (Brünger et al., 1987; Brunger and Adams, 2002) is used to enhance local map-model agreement (e.g. side chain rotamers), while keeping well-refined parts of the model unchanged.
evidence: The Results section describes the use of simulated annealing with citations.

claim: The X-ray structure of a rabbit muscle aldolase (PDB ID: 6ALD) was used as the starting model for refinement into the cryo-EM map (EMD ID: 8743, PDB ID: 5VY5).
source: To this end, our method was applied to fit the X-ray structure of a rabbit muscle aldolase (PDB ID: 6ALD; Choi et al., 1999) to the recently deposited data set (EMD ID: 8743, PDB ID: 5VY5; Herzik et al., 2017).
evidence: The Results section describes the aldolase test case with citations.

claim: Higher resolution X-ray structures (PDB IDs: 3BV4 at 1.7 Å, 1ZAH at 1.8 Å, 1ADO at 1.9 Å) were used to validate the aldolase results.
source: Higher resolution X-ray structures were used to validate the results (PDB IDs: 3BV4 at 1.7 Å (Sherawat et al., 2008); 1ZAH at 1.8 Å (St-Jean et al., 2005); 1ADO at 1.9 Å (Blom and Sygusch, 1997)).
evidence: The Results section describes the validation structures with citations.

claim: The starting model for aldolase was first refined against a training map reconstructed from half of the raw cryo-EM images (half-map), while simultaneously cross-validating against a validation map (the other half-map).
source: Following the standard approach to avoid overfitting (Amunts et al., 2014; Brown et al., 2015), we first refined the starting model against a training map reconstructed from half of the raw cryo-EM images (half-map), while simultaneously cross-validating against a validation map (the other half-map) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: The Results section describes the half-map validation approach with citations and references a figure.

claim: The target force constant for aldolase refinement was set to 5 × 10^5 kJ mol^-1 which was roughly 10% of the total system energy.
source: The target force constant was set to 5 × 105 kJ mol-1 which was roughly 10% of the total system energy and was a good initial guess.
evidence: The Results section describes the force constant used.

claim: During the half-map refinement of aldolase, the fitted model converged to a structure with RMSDref ≈2 Å.
source: Already during the half-map refinement the fitted model converged to a structure with RMSDref ≈2 Å.
evidence: The Results section describes the convergence of the aldolase refinement.

claim: No large differences were observed between FSCtrain and FSCval at any point during the half-map refinement of aldolase, confirming the absence of overfitting.
source: No large differences were observed between FSCtrain and FSCval at any point during the half-map refinement, confirming the absence of overfitting.
evidence: The Results section describes the cross-validation results.

claim: Additional refinement including simulated annealing against the full map for aldolase brought RMSDref further down to ∼1.8 Å.
source: Finally, we performed additional refinement including simulated annealing against the full map to account for features not present in the training map, which brought RMSDref further down to ∼1.8 Å.
evidence: The Results section describes the full map refinement results.

claim: CDMD refinement of aldolase converged quickly to a state being very close to the deposited reference and showed a significant improvement of the refined model both in geometry and reciprocal-space correlation relative to the starting structure.
source: CDMD refinement converged quickly to a state being very close to the deposited reference and showed a significant improvement of the refined model both in geometry and reciprocal-space correlation relative to the starting structure (Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The Results section summarizes the aldolase refinement results and references figures.

claim: Only Rosetta was able to converge as close to the reference as CDMD for aldolase, yielding a structure with good geometry.
source: Only Rosetta was able to converge as close to the reference as our method, yielding a structure with good geometry, while neither Phenix nor Refmac was.
evidence: The Results section compares CDMD with alternative methods.

claim: Refinement with Phenix for aldolase produced reasonable geometry but showed poor convergence of solvent-exposed flexible loops.
source: Refinement with Phenix produced reasonable geometry but showed poor convergence of solvent-exposed flexible loops, which contributed to the larger RMSDref.
evidence: The Results section describes the Phenix refinement results.

claim: Refinement with Refmac for aldolase did not place those protein regions into the density that showed the largest RMSDref prior to refinement and produced rather poor geometry.
source: Refinement with Refmac did not place those protein regions into the density that showed the largest RMSDref prior to refinement (see Figure 3a) and produced rather poor geometry.
evidence: The Results section describes the Refmac refinement results and references a figure.

claim: Neither the CDMD model nor the deposited reference for aldolase showed a considerably smaller RMSD value to any of the control structures, suggesting that both models might be equally good approximations of the 'true structure'.
source: Neither model showed a considerably smaller RMSD value to any of the control structures, suggesting that both models might be equally good approximations of the 'true structure'.
evidence: The Results section compares the models to control structures.

claim: The aldolase results suggest that CDMD is capable of correcting structural errors and converges quickly to the target state while maintaining good geometry at all refinement stages.
source: Overall, the aldolase results suggest that CDMD is capable of correcting structural errors and converges quickly to the target state while maintaining good geometry at all refinement stages.
evidence: The Results section summarizes the aldolase results.

claim: CDMD was applied to a medium-resolution map (4.1 Å) of a GDP-tubulin dimer in the straight microtubule-like conformation.
source: We next applied CDMD to a medium-resolution map (4.1 Å) of a GDP-tubulin dimer in the straight microtubule-like conformation derived from an asymmetric helical reconstruction of a complete, kinesin-decorated microtubule lattice (provided by courtesy of Zhang and Nogales, 2015).
evidence: The Results section describes the tubulin test case with citation.

claim: Two high-resolution GDP-tubulin structures (PDB ID: 3JAS at 3.3 Å and PDB ID: 6DPV at 3.5 Å) in the same conformational state were used as controls for tubulin.
source: However, two high-resolution GDP-tubulin structures (PDB ID: 3JAS at 3.3 Å and PDB ID: 6DPV at 3.5 Å) in the same conformational state were available (Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018). We used these structures as controls to confirm the method's accuracy and convergence for medium-resolution maps.
evidence: The Results section describes the control structures with citations.

claim: The CDMD model for tubulin reached the same reciprocal-space correlation with the full map across the whole range of spatial frequencies as the high-resolution control structures, despite the higher accuracy of the control structures.
source: Despite the higher accuracy of the control structures, our model reached the same reciprocal-space correlation with the full map across the whole range of spatial frequencies (Figure 4b, top).
evidence: The Results section describes the map-model agreement and references a figure.

claim: The good correlation of the CDMD tubulin model did not result from overfitting or geometry violations as confirmed by the cross-validation procedure and stereochemical quality assessment.
source: The good correlation did not result from overfitting or geometry violations as confirmed by the cross-validation procedure (as in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, data not shown) and stereochemical quality assessment (Figure 4b, bottom).
evidence: The Results section describes the validation results and references figures.

claim: The CDMD tubulin model was very similar in stereochemical quality to the control structures except for the ∼10-fold smaller number of steric clashes and a higher fraction of Ramachandran outliers.
source: Our model was very similar in stereochemical quality to the control structures except for the ∼10-fold smaller number of steric clashes and a higher fraction of Ramachandran outliers.
evidence: The Results section compares the model quality.

claim: The higher EMRinger score for the CDMD tubulin model indicated improved local side chain correlations and backbone placement.
source: The higher EMRinger score for our model indicated improved local side chain correlations and backbone placement.
evidence: The Results section describes the EMRinger score.

claim: CDMD refinement of tubulin quickly converged to the straight state that was very similar in RMSD to the control structures.
source: As in the aldolase case, CDMD refinement quickly converged to the straight state that was very similar in RMSD to the control structures (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The Results section describes the convergence and references a figure.

claim: Among all the methods tested for tubulin, only Phenix produced a structure with comparable geometry and map agreement as the CDMD model.
source: Among all the methods tested, only Phenix produced a structure with comparable geometry and map agreement as our model.
evidence: The Results section compares CDMD with alternative methods.

claim: Rosetta and Refmac showed poorer convergence in more flexible loop regions for tubulin, with the Rosetta model having a much higher number of steric clashes.
source: Rosetta and Refmac showed poorer convergence in more flexible loop regions, with the Rosetta model having a much higher number of steric clashes.
evidence: The Results section describes the alternative methods' results.

claim: The tubulin refinements demonstrate the accuracy and good convergence of CDMD at medium resolutions, namely its ability to provide plausible local geometries in cases where this information is not fully present in the map and the refinement has to partially rely on the force field.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate the accuracy and good convergence of CDMD at medium resolutions, namely its ability to provide plausible local geometries in cases where this information is not fully present in the map and the refinement has to partially rely on the force field.
evidence: The Results section summarizes the tubulin results.

claim: CDMD was applied to the vanilloid receptor 1 (TRPV1) resolved at 3.2 Å (EMD ID: 5778, PDB ID: 3J5P) for which the local resolution ranged from 2.5 to 7 Å.
source: Our next test system was the vanilloid receptor 1 (TRPV1) resolved at 3.2 Å (EMD ID: 5778, PDB ID: 3J5P; Liao et al., 2013) for which the local resolution ranged from 2.5 to 7 Å, such that no standard non-MD refinement algorithm could be applied to fit a distant model uniformly well to all map regions.
evidence: The Results section describes the TRPV1 test case with citation.

claim: The large difference in the local resolution of TRPV1 is due to a rigid transmembrane (TM) domain and flexible, cytosolic ankyrin repeat domains (ARDs).
source: The large difference in the local resolution is due to a rigid transmembrane (TM) domain and flexible, cytosolic ankyrin repeat domains (ARDs) (Liao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section explains the local resolution variation with citations.

claim: Residues 111–198 of the ARDs in TRPV1 were only poorly reflected in the density.
source: It should also be noted that residues 111–198 of the ARDs were only poorly reflected in the density.
evidence: The Results section describes the density quality.

claim: The CDMD model for TRPV1 correlated better with the full map at spatial frequencies below 0.1 Å^-1 (better rigid-body positioning of the domains) but worse in the 0.2–0.3 Å^-1 range compared to the deposited reference structure.
source: Unlike in the above cases, our model correlated better with the full map at spatial frequencies below 0.1 Å-1 (better rigid-body positioning of the domains) but worse in the 0.2–0.3 Å-1 range (Figure 5b, top).
evidence: The Results section describes the map-model agreement and references a figure.

claim: The CDMD model for TRPV1 was systematically better in all quality statistics except for a moderate fraction of Ramachandran outliers compared to the deposited reference.
source: This was further supported by the model quality assessment (Figure 5b, bottom), where our model was systematically better in all quality statistics except for a moderate fraction of Ramachandran outliers.
evidence: The Results section describes the model quality and references a figure.

claim: CDMD refinement of TRPV1 converged to a structure with good geometry and RMSDref ≈2.5 Å, while the other methods did not.
source: CDMD refinement converged to a structure with good geometry and RMSDref ≈2.5 Å, while the other methods did not.
evidence: The Results section describes the convergence results.

claim: The convergence of TRPV1 refinement was good in the well-resolved TM region across all methods, but only Refmac was able to place the flexible ARD regions back into the density (RMSDref ≈2.8 Å), however, at the price of severe geometry violations.
source: The convergence was good in the well-resolved TM region across all methods, but only Refmac was able to place the flexible ARD regions back into the density (RMSDref ≈2.8 Å), however, at the price of severe geometry violations.
evidence: The Results section describes the alternative methods' results.

claim: Phenix and Rosetta yielded accurate models for TRPV1 but were unable to refine solvent-exposed flexible loops in the ARD region.
source: Phenix and Rosetta yielded accurate models but were unable to refine solvent-exposed flexible loops in the ARD region.
evidence: The Results section describes the alternative methods' results.

claim: Three independent refinements of TRPV1 produce very similar models but the structural variability was larger in the ARDs, whereas the refinements converged to almost the same structure in the TM domain, consistent with the local resolution in these regions.
source: We found that all three refinements produce very similar models but the structural variability was larger in the ARDs, whereas the refinements converged to almost the same structure in the TM domain, consistent with the local resolution in these regions (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The Results section describes the reproducibility and references a figure.

claim: The TRPV1 refinements demonstrate that CDMD has a large and robust radius of convergence and is able to significantly improve poor starting models irrespective of local resolution and within a single refinement run.
source: In summary, the TRPV1 refinements demonstrate that CDMD has a large and robust radius of convergence and is able to significantly improve poor starting models irrespective of local resolution and within a single refinement run.
evidence: The Results section summarizes the TRPV1 results.

claim: The TRPV1 system has been previously used to benchmark the Rosetta and ReMDFF algorithms.
source: The TRPV1 system has been previously used to benchmark the Rosetta (Wang et al., 2016a) and ReMDFF (Singharoy et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018) algorithms, which offers an additional comparison to these methods.
evidence: The Results section describes the comparison with citations.

claim: The Rosetta model for TRPV1 (PDB ID: 3J9J) contained only the TM region.
source: However, the Rosetta model (PDB ID: 3J9J; Barad et al., 2015) contained only the TM region, whereas only one TRPV1 monomer was refined with ReMDFF (courtesy by Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: The Results section describes the Rosetta model with citation.

claim: Only one TRPV1 monomer was refined with ReMDFF.
source: However, the Rosetta model (PDB ID: 3J9J; Barad et al., 2015) contained only the TM region, whereas only one TRPV1 monomer was refined with ReMDFF (courtesy by Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: The Results section describes the ReMDFF model with citation.

claim: The CDMD model for the TM region of TRPV1 compared well with that generated by Rosetta both in terms of reciprocal-space correlation and model quality.
source: As shown in Figure 6b, our model for the TM region compared well with that generated by Rosetta both in terms of reciprocal-space correlation and model quality.
evidence: The Results section describes the comparison and references a figure.

claim: In the ReMDFF comparison for TRPV1, the CDMD model outperformed the ReMDFF model both in reciprocal-space correlation and model geometry.
source: In the ReMDFF comparison, our model outperformed the ReMDFF model both in reciprocal-space correlation and model geometry (Figure 6d).
evidence: The Results section describes the comparison and references a figure.

claim: The CDMD model for TRPV1 outperformed the ReMDFF model mainly due to better map-model agreement in the low-resolution ARD region.
source: This was mainly due to better map-model agreement of our model in the low-resolution ARD region (Figure 6c, bottom insert), which was confirmed by the higher reciprocal correlation values at low spatial frequencies (Figure 6d, top).
evidence: The Results section explains the difference and references figures.

claim: Much poorer rotamer and Ramachandran distributions were observed for the ReMDFF model for TRPV1 despite the fact that, like CDMD, ReMDFF employs an accurate atomistic force field.
source: We also observed much poorer rotamer and Ramachandran distributions for the ReMDFF model (Figure 6d, bottom) despite the fact that, like our method, ReMDFF employs an accurate atomistic force field.
evidence: The Results section describes the model quality and references a figure.

claim: CDMD was compared with the newest Phenix protocol on a system that has been recently refined using optimized refinement parameters.
source: Further to the previous section, we compared how CDMD performs on a system that has been recently refined using the newest Phenix protocol (Afonine et al., 2018) with optimized refinement parameters (White et al., 2018).
evidence: The Results section describes the comparison with citations.

claim: The structure of an ATP-bound NSF (PDB ID: 3J94) was refined into the ∼3.9 Å map of a NSF complex (EMD ID: 9102, class 1).
source: To this end, the structure of an ATP-bound NSF (PDB ID: 3J94; Zhao et al., 2015) was refined into the ∼3.9 Å map of a NSF complex (EMD ID: 9102, class 1; White et al., 2018).
evidence: The Results section describes the NSF test case with citations.

claim: The starting structure for NSF was completed to match the deposited Phenix model.
source: To enable a direct comparison, the starting structure was completed to match the deposited Phenix model (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The Results section describes the starting model preparation.

claim: Higher-resolution X-ray structures (PDB IDs: 1NSF at 1.9 Å; 1D2N at 1.75 Å) were used to validate the NSF results.
source: Higher-resolution X-ray structures were used to validate the results (PDB IDs: 1NSF at 1.9 Å (Yu et al., 1998); 1D2N at 1.75 Å (Lenzen et al., 1998)).
evidence: The Results section describes the validation structures with citations.

claim: No half-maps were available for the NSF test case, which precluded the half-map-based cross-validation and, hence, determining the optimal force constant.
source: No half-maps were available for this test case, which precluded the half-map-based cross-validation and, hence, determining the optimal force constant.
evidence: The Results section describes the limitation of the NSF test case.

claim: The map-model agreement for NSF improved gradually as the target force constant increased, but the final models correlated almost equally well with the full map.
source: The map-model agreement improved gradually as the target force constant increased, but the final models correlated almost equally well with the full map (Figure 7b, top, red curves).
evidence: The Results section describes the refinement results and references a figure.

claim: The CDMD model for NSF had a substantially lower clashscore compared to the deposited reference.
source: Comparison of our NSF model with the deposited reference revealed that it had a substantially lower clashscore (Figure 7b, bottom), which might be attributed to the use of an accurate force field that improved poorly defined regions.
evidence: The Results section describes the model quality and references a figure.

claim: The CDMD model for NSF showed systematically lower RMSD values to both control structures (roughly a 0.2 Å difference) compared to the deposited reference.
source: Our NSF model showed systematically lower RMSD values to both controls (roughly a 0.2 Å difference, which is detectable given the small size of the compared structures).
evidence: The Results section compares the models to control structures.

claim: The difference in RMSD for NSF was mainly explained by the difference in the ATP binding pockets and the CDMD model more closely resembled the control structures in this region.
source: Visual inspection revealed that this was mainly explained by the difference in the ATP binding pockets and that our model more closely resembled the control structures in this region.
evidence: The Results section explains the difference.

claim: A proper treatment of electrostatics is important for correct ligand placement in the absence of sufficient density information.
source: We speculate that a proper treatment of electrostatics is important for correct ligand placement in the absence of sufficient density information.
evidence: The Results section speculates on the importance of electrostatics.

claim: None of the alternative refinement methods for NSF was able to approach the reference structure demonstrating only ∼0.5 Å of improvement in terms of RMSDref as compared to ∼2 Å of improvement by CDMD.
source: Unlike in the above test cases, none of the alternative refinement methods was able to approach the reference structure demonstrating only ∼0.5 Å of improvement in terms of RMSDref as compared to ∼2 Å of improvement by CDMD.
evidence: The Results section compares CDMD with alternative methods.

claim: The convergence of NSF refinement was better in the D2 domain for all alternative methods than in the D1 domain, where the split region between protomers A and F and the SNAP-25A 17 N-terminal residues were only poorly modelled by Phenix, Rosetta and Refmac.
source: Interestingly, the convergence was better in the D2 domain for all alternative methods than in the D1 domain, where the split region between protomers A and F and the SNAP-25A 17 N-terminal residues were only poorly modelled by Phenix, Rosetta and Refmac.
evidence: The Results section describes the alternative methods' results.

claim: For the alternative methods, the hexagonal symmetry of the D2 domain translated into global symmetry restraints improves the refinement of this part of the NSF complex relative to the D1 domain, where the symmetry is broken by the split region.
source: We speculate that, for the alternative methods, the hexagonal symmetry of the D2 domain translated into global symmetry restraints improves the refinement of this part of the NSF complex relative to the D1 domain, where the symmetry is broken by the split region.
evidence: The Results section speculates on the reason for the difference.

claim: CDMD does not need symmetry restraints (or any other geometry-based restraints) and relies solely on the interatomic interactions defined by the force field.
source: Here, we again emphasize that CDMD does not need symmetry restraints (or any other geometry-based restraints) and relies solely on the interatomic interactions defined by the force field.
evidence: The Results section emphasizes a feature of CDMD.

claim: The low-resolution structure of a 'breathing' nucleosome complex (PDB ID: 6ESI) was refined into the 3.7 Å map of the canonical nucleosome state (EMD ID: 3947, PDB ID: 6ESF).
source: To this end, we refined the recently published low-resolution structure of a 'breathing' nucleosome complex (PDB ID: 6ESI; Bilokapic et al., 2018) into the 3.7 Å map of the canonical nucleosome state (EMD ID: 3947, PDB ID: 6ESF; Bilokapic et al., 2018).
evidence: The Results section describes the nucleosome test case with citations.

claim: The major rearrangements between the two nucleosome states include a contraction along the symmetry axis coupled to a concomitant expansion in the perpendicular direction and a shift by ∼1 base pair in the DNA due to rearrangements in the histone-DNA interface.
source: The major rearrangements between the two states include a contraction along the symmetry axis coupled to a concomitant expansion in the perpendicular direction and a shift by ∼1 base pair in the DNA due to rearrangements in the histone-DNA interface.
evidence: The Results section describes the conformational changes.

claim: The following higher-quality X-ray structures of the canonical nucleosome state were used to validate the nucleosome results: 1KX3 at 1.9 Å and 5OMX at 2.3 Å for the histone part only, and 5MLU at 2.8 Å for the DNA part.
source: We used the following higher-quality X-ray structures of the canonical nucleosome state to validate the results: 1KX3 at 1.9 Å (Davey et al., 2002) and 5OMX at 2.3 Å (Frouws et al., 2018) for the histone part only (due to different DNA sequences), and 5MLU at 2.8 Å (Makde et al., 2010) for the DNA part.
evidence: The Results section describes the validation structures with citations.

claim: Both the CDMD model and the deposited reference for nucleosome correlated almost equally well with the full map.
source: Both models correlated almost equally well with the full map (Figure 8b, top), with the deposited model correlating slightly better at spatial frequencies above 0.2 Å-1, which again raised the question of underfitting as in the case of the TRPV1 refinement (see previous section).
evidence: The Results section describes the map-model agreement and references a figure.

claim: The goodness-of-fit for nucleosome slowly improved as the force constant increased, but the refined structure never reached the same extent of reciprocal-space correlation as the deposited reference, suggesting that the deposited reference structure might be slightly overfitting the full map.
source: The goodness-of-fit slowly improved as the force constant increased, but the refined structure never reached the same extent of reciprocal-space correlation as the deposited reference, suggesting that the deposited reference structure might be slightly overfitting the full map.
evidence: The Results section infers overfitting based on the refinement results.

claim: The CDMD model for nucleosome showed a systematic improvement relative to both starting and deposited reference structure, except for a moderate fraction of Ramachandran outliers and a slightly lower EMRinger score.
source: This conclusion was also supported by the model quality statistics (Figure 8b, bottom) which showed a systematic improvement of our model relative to both starting and deposited reference structure, except for a moderate fraction of Ramachandran outliers and a slightly lower EMRinger score.
evidence: The Results section describes the model quality and references a figure.

claim: Neither the CDMD model nor the deposited reference for nucleosome had systematically lower RMSD values to both control structures, suggesting that both models are good representations of the 'true structure'.
source: As in the aldolase case, neither model had systematically lower RMSD values to both control structures, suggesting that both models are good representations of the 'true structure'.
evidence: The Results section compares the models to control structures.

claim: The DNA part of the nucleosome was very similar across all models: RMSDcontrol ≈1.4 Å for both the CDMD model and the reference, and RMSD less than 0.9 Å between the compared models themselves.
source: The DNA part was very similar across all models: RMSDcontrol ≈1.4 Å for both our model and the reference, and RMSD less than 0.9 Å between the compared models themselves (all DNA non-hydrogen atoms).
evidence: The Results section describes the DNA quality.

claim: The DNA accuracy in the deposited nucleosome reference (refined with Phenix) was due to the use of base-pairing and base-stacking restraints and a much closer starting structure.
source: It should be noted that the DNA accuracy in the deposited reference (refined with Phenix) was due to the use of base-pairing and base-stacking restraints and a much closer starting structure.
evidence: The Results section explains the DNA accuracy in the reference.

claim: The high level of achieved DNA quality in the CDMD nucleosome model is particularly remarkable because (a) no geometry restraints were used, and (b) the CHARMM force field family used to refine the nucleosome is rather inaccurate in reproducing correct nucleotide base pairing when used in plain MD simulations.
source: On the contrary, the high level of achieved DNA quality in our model is particularly remarkable because (a) no geometry restraints were used, and (b) the CHARMM force field family used to refine the nucleosome (see Materials and methods) is rather inaccurate in reproducing correct nucleotide base pairing when used in plain MD simulations (Galindo-Murillo et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section highlights the DNA quality with citation.

claim: The 'soft' (global) fitting potential with a well-adjusted weight is a substantial factor in maintaining the modelled structure's accuracy, even in cases where neither the resolution nor the structural knowledge (e.g. a force field) are satisfactory.
source: We hence conclude that the 'soft' (global) fitting potential (Figure 1) with a well-adjusted weight is a substantial factor in maintaining the modelled structure's accuracy, even in cases where neither the resolution nor the structural knowledge (e.g. a force field) are satisfactory.
evidence: The Results section concludes based on the nucleosome results and references a figure.

claim: Among all the methods tested for nucleosome, only CDMD was able to achieve a model accuracy and map-model agreement similar to the deposited reference.
source: Among all the methods tested, only CDMD was able to achieve a model accuracy and map-model agreement similar to the deposited reference.
evidence: The Results section compares CDMD with alternative methods.

claim: Although the histone part of nucleosome was refined similarly well by all of the methods, the DNA part was, if anything, only poorly refined (Refmac) and in most cases disintegrated (Phenix and Rosetta).
source: Although the histone part was refined similarly well by all of the methods, the DNA part was, if anything, only poorly refined (Refmac) and in most cases disintegrated (Phenix and Rosetta).
evidence: The Results section describes the alternative methods' results.

claim: The poor DNA quality of the Rosetta nucleosome model is likely due to the internal Rosetta energy function that was originally designed for protein modeling, and a generalization for RNA/DNA is currently being developed.
source: The poor DNA quality of the Rosetta model is likely due to the internal Rosetta energy function that was originally designed for protein modeling (Alford et al., 2017), and a generalization for RNA/DNA is currently being developed.
evidence: The Results section explains the Rosetta results with citation.

claim: The fact that the Phenix refinement of nucleosome, in which DNA restraints were constantly switched on, was unable to converge to the reference structure might indicate that the starting structure is out of this method's radius of convergence.
source: The fact that the Phenix refinement, in which DNA restraints were constantly switched on, was unable to converge to the reference structure might indicate that the starting structure is out of this method's radius of convergence.
evidence: The Results section infers the limitation of Phenix.

claim: For Refmac refinement of nucleosome, the optimal geometry weights necessary to obtain good agreement for the DNA and the histone part differed by 2–3 orders of magnitude such that a refinement of the entire nucleosome structure in a single run was impossible without severe geometry violations.
source: For Refmac, the optimal geometry weights necessary to obtain good agreement for the DNA and the histone part differed by 2–3 orders of magnitude such that a refinement of the entire nucleosome structure in a single run was impossible without severe geometry violations.
evidence: The Results section describes the Refmac results.

claim: The medium-resolution structure (PDB ID: 3JCF) of a magnesium transporter CorA in the closed, symmetric Mg2+-bound state was refined into a 7.1 Å subclass map (EMD ID: 6552; PDB ID: 3JCG, backbone model only) of one of the Mg2+-free, asymmetric open states.
source: To this end, we refined the medium-resolution structure (PDB ID: 3JCF; Matthies et al., 2016) of a magnesium transporter CorA in the closed, symmetric Mg2+-bound state into a 7.1 Å subclass map (EMD ID: 6552; PDB ID: 3JCG, backbone model only) of one of the Mg2+-free, asymmetric open states.
evidence: The Results section describes the CorA test case with citations.

claim: The CorA results were compared with models produced by MDFF, a well-established tool originally designed for exactly such refinement cases.
source: We additionally compared our results with CorA models produced by MDFF, a well-established tool originally designed for exactly such refinement cases (see Materials and methods for the MDFF protocol).
evidence: The Results section describes the comparison with MDFF.

claim: Both the CDMD model and the one refined with MDFF for CorA correlated similarly well with the low-resolution map, with the latter correlating better at spatial frequencies above 0.1 Å^-1 (irrespective of whether or not secondary structure restraints were enabled).
source: Both our model and the one refined with MDFF correlated similarly well with the low-resolution map, with the latter correlating better at spatial frequencies above 0.1 Å-1 (irrespective of whether or not secondary structure restraints were enabled).
evidence: The Results section describes the map-model agreement.

claim: The quality of the MDFF models for CorA was systematically lower than that of the CDMD models, although each model had almost zero steric clashes (due to the use of an atomistic force field).
source: However, the quality of the MDFF models was systematically lower than that of our models (Figure 10b,c, bottom and Figure 10—figure supplement 1), although each model had almost zero steric clashes (due to the use of an atomistic force field).
evidence: The Results section describes the model quality and references figures.

claim: The quality of the MDFF model for CorA decreased as the restraints were released.
source: The quality of the MDFF model decreased as the restraints were released (Figure 10c and Figure 10—figure supplement 1, blue vs. dark blue).
evidence: The Results section describes the effect of restraints and references figures.

claim: The gating pore of the CDMD CorA model was, on average, wider along the pathway than that of the closed symmetric structure.
source: The gating pore of our CorA model was, on average, wider along the pathway than that of the closed symmetric structure.
evidence: The Results section describes the gating pore structure.

claim: The average solvent density in the gating pore of the CDMD CorA model was lower, consistent with the increased pore volume.
source: The average solvent density in the gating pore of our CorA model was lower, consistent with the increased pore volume.
evidence: The Results section describes the solvent density.

claim: The gating pore in the MDFF model for CorA was rather curled and significantly smaller in volume than that of the closed symmetric structure, despite the intracellular stalk helices adopting an asymmetric conformation very similar to the CDMD model.
source: Surprisingly, the gating pore in the MDFF model was rather curled and significantly smaller in volume than that of the closed symmetric structure, despite the intracellular stalk helices adopting an asymmetric conformation very similar to our model.
evidence: The Results section describes the MDFF model structure.

claim: The gate closure in the central part of the transmembrane domain in the MDFF CorA model led to a complete permeation block as indicated by zero number density in this region (no water molecules were present).
source: It was mainly due to the gate closure in the central part of the transmembrane domain (pore radii reaching 0.5 Å, see Figure 10—figure supplement 3) that led to a complete permeation block as indicated by zero number density in this region (no water molecules were present).
evidence: The Results section describes the gate closure and references a figure.

claim: The conformation of the gating pore in the MDFF CorA model would lead to even weaker conductance than in the case of the closed symmetric channel in free MD simulations.
source: We speculate that this conformation of the gating pore in the MDFF model would lead to even weaker conductance than in the case of the closed symmetric channel in free MD simulations.
evidence: The Results section speculates on the conductance.

claim: The fact that the gating pore opens and is on average more solvated in the CDMD fitting simulations for CorA is in agreement with previous biochemical and simulation data.
source: Although a higher-resolution control is still required to validate the open structure produced by CDMD, the fact that the gating pore opens and is on average more solvated in the CDMD fitting simulations is in agreement with previous biochemical and simulation data (Chakrabarti et al., 2010; Dalmas et al., 2014).
evidence: The Results section compares the results with previous data with citations.

claim: MDFF was unable to induce gate opening for CorA.
source: Remarkably, MDFF was unable to induce gate opening.
evidence: The Results section describes the MDFF results.

claim: Switching off all the restraints in MDFF for CorA did not lead to gate opening either.
source: To test whether it is the secondary structure restraints (an option strongly recommended for low-resolution refinement with MDFF) that prevented the torque generated by rearranging the intracellular domains from propagating into the gate region, we switched off all the restraints and re-refined the starting structure. This restraint-free MDFF setup did not lead to gate opening either (Figure 10—figure supplement 2, rightmost structure; Figure 10—figure supplement 3, bottom right plot).
evidence: The Results section describes the restraint-free MDFF results and references figures.

claim: It is the 'hard' MDFF biasing potential (each density grid point is an attractor) that makes the refined model less compliant and restricted only to the highest-density regions.
source: We therefore speculate that it is the 'hard' MDFF biasing potential (each density grid point is an attractor) that makes the refined model less compliant and restricted only to the highest-density regions.
evidence: The Results section speculates on the reason for the difference.

claim: The 'soft' correlation-based potential (global map-model overlap is maximized) allows more internal flexibility while maintaining a comparable degree of map-model agreement.
source: On the contrary, the 'soft' correlation-based potential (global map-model overlap is maximized) allows more internal flexibility while maintaining a comparable degree of map-model agreement (Figure 10b,c, top, and Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The Results section describes the advantage of the correlation-based potential and references figures.

claim: When coupled to a stereochemically accurate treatment (atomistic force field), the CDMD refinement protocol might be useful in modeling biologically relevant transitions.
source: When coupled to a stereochemically accurate treatment (atomistic force field), our refinement protocol might thus be useful in modeling biologically relevant transitions.
evidence: The Results section suggests a potential application.

claim: In many of the test cases, the remarkable reduction of steric clashes by CDMD often comes at the cost of increased rotamer and/or Ramachandran outliers, as compared to the deposited reference models.
source: We now return to the question of why in many of the above test cases the remarkable reduction of steric clashes by CDMD often comes at the cost of increased rotamer and/or Ramachandran outliers, as compared to the deposited reference models (Figure 3, Figure 4, Figure 6a,b, Figure 7, Figure 9).
evidence: The Results section raises a question and references figures.

claim: By construction, the refinement methods used to produce the deposited models (COOT, Phenix, Rosetta, Refmac) often enforce accurate rotamer and Ramachandran distributions, whereas, also by construction, force-field-based refinement guarantees almost zero steric clashes.
source: It should be first noted that, by construction, the refinement methods used to produce the deposited models (COOT, Phenix, Rosetta, Refmac) often enforce accurate rotamer and Ramachandran distributions, whereas, also by construction, force-field-based refinement guarantees almost zero steric clashes.
evidence: The Results section explains the difference in refinement methods.

claim: The structural errors observed in CDMD models may (a) arise due to imperfections of the force fields in use, (b) be enforced by the cryo-EM data (real or noise), or (c) be a synergetic combination of these effects.
source: The question therefore narrows down to whether the structural errors observed in our models (a) arise due to imperfections of the force fields in use (e.g., inaccurate backbone dihedral, rotamer torsion angles or atomic partial charges), (b) are enforced by the cryo-EM data (real or noise), or (c) are a synergetic combination of these effects.
evidence: The Results section poses hypotheses about the source of errors.

claim: There was an overall decrease both in the average per-residue outlier propensity and in the total outlier occurrence after CDMD refinement, irrespective of the force field.
source: We first asked if our refinement procedure (Figure 1 and Figure 2) per se improves the rotamer and Ramachandran distributions. Indeed, there was an overall decrease both in the average per-residue outlier propensity and in the total outlier occurrence (Figure 11, gray vs. blue or red dots), irrespective of the force field.
evidence: The Results section describes the per-residue analysis and references figures.

claim: A considerable fraction of structural conflicts is resolved by the CDMD refinement and the cryo-EM density improves the geometry of initially poorer models leaving a certain number of residue-unspecific outliers.
source: These data indicate that a considerable fraction of structural conflicts is resolved by the refinement and support scenario (b) above: that the cryo-EM density improves the geometry of initially poorer models leaving a certain number of residue-unspecific outliers.
evidence: The Results section interprets the per-residue analysis.

claim: For the non-ribosome systems refined using CHARMM22*/CHARMM36m, aspartates, leucines, tryptophans and valines contributed most to the overall outlier occurrences, which, however, remained rather low (outlier propensities of ∼0.04 or lower).
source: In particular, for the non-ribosome systems refined using CHARMM22*/CHARMM36m (Piana et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2017), aspartates, leucines, tryptophans and valines contributed most to the overall outlier occurrences, which, however, remained rather low (outlier propensities of ∼0.04 or lower).
evidence: The Results section describes the per-residue analysis with citations.

claim: AMBER12sb force field used for the ribosome refinement performed similarly to CHARMM22*/CHARMM36m for all rotamer types except for threonines and valines which systematically disagreed with their knowledge-based conformations (an order of magnitude higher outlier propensities, ∼0.33 and ∼0.2, respectively).
source: AMBER12sb (Lindorff-Larsen et al., 2010) force field used for the ribosome refinement performed similarly to CHARMM22*/CHARMM36m for all rotamer types except for threonines and valines which systematically disagreed with their knowledge-based conformations (an order of magnitude higher outlier propensities, ∼0.33 and ∼0.2, respectively).
evidence: The Results section describes the per-residue analysis with citation.

claim: The presence of systematic structure errors supports the scenario that the structural errors detected in CDMD models are residue- and force-field-specific and not corrected by the refinement.
source: The presence of systematic structure errors, therefore, supports scenario (a) as these errors are residue- and force-field-specific and not corrected by the refinement.
evidence: The Results section interprets the per-residue analysis.

claim: There are several lines of evidence that the structural errors detected in CDMD models are likely to be a combination of cryo-EM data-specific outliers and force field artifacts.
source: Thus, there are several lines of evidence that the structural errors detected in our models are likely to be a combination of cryo-EM data-specific outliers and force field artifacts (scenario (c) above).
evidence: The Results section concludes based on the per-residue analysis.

claim: The quality of a refined structure is only as good as the experimentally determined map.
source: It should be noted that the quality of a refined structure is only as good as the experimentally determined map.
evidence: The Results section states a general principle.

claim: Low determinacy of 3D classification and poor alignment of cryo-EM particles may be related to the non-ideal nature of structure refinement.
source: Low determinacy of 3D classification and poor alignment of cryo-EM particles may be related to the non-ideal nature of structure refinement.
evidence: The Results section discusses potential sources of errors.

claim: Conformational heterogeneity and ensemble averaging misinterpreted as a single structure can be another source of structural errors in which case an ensemble refinement may be required.
source: Furthermore, conformational heterogeneity and ensemble averaging misinterpreted as a single structure can be another source of structural errors in which case an ensemble refinement may be required (Rice et al., 1998; Burnley et al., 2012; Herzik et al., 2019; Bonomi et al., 2018).
evidence: The Results section discusses potential sources of errors with citations.

claim: In the present study, the authors have concentrated on single-structure refinement and have implicitly assumed that each map stems from a unique conformational state of the biological complex in question.
source: In our present study, we have concentrated on single-structure refinement and have implicitly assumed that each map stems from a unique conformational state of the biological complex in question.
evidence: The Results section describes the scope of the study.

claim: The assumption that each map stems from a unique conformational state is a good approximation for high-resolution maps.
source: This is a good approximation for high-resolution maps (e.g. Figure 3).
evidence: The Results section states an assumption and references a figure.

claim: For medium- and low-resolution maps, the best representation might not be a single structure but rather a weighted set of structures.
source: For medium- and low-resolution maps, the best representation might not be a single structure but rather a weighted set of structures.
evidence: The Results section discusses the limitation of single-structure refinement.

claim: The TRPV1 system is an example where the best representation might not be a single structure but rather a weighted set of structures.
source: The TRPV1 system (Figure 5) is one example of such a case in our study. Here, three independent refinements produced three structures with very similar conformations in the high-resolution TM region and with much more variability in the low-resolution ARD domains (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The Results section provides an example and references figures.

claim: Correction of the force-field outliers is tightly linked to the general force field development.
source: Correction of the force-field outliers, in turn, is tightly linked to the general force field development.
evidence: The Results section discusses force field development.

claim: It is well known what the expectations are for structural errors such as steric clashes, rotamer and Ramachandran statistics, Cβ deviations, chirality errors, etc.
source: On the one hand, it is well known what the expectations are for such errors (Bower et al., 1997; Shapovalov and Dunbrack, 2011; Renfrew et al., 2008; Towse et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section cites references to support this claim.

claim: Incorporation of knowledge about structural errors into the force field development is challenging as it fundamentally differs from the way a rotameric library is constructed.
source: On the other hand, incorporation of this knowledge into the force field development is challenging as it fundamentally differs from the way a rotameric library is constructed (Towse et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section cites a reference to support this claim.

claim: The results clearly imply that the correlation-driven MD refinement is able to generate models with a quality consistent with well-established methods given the map quality.
source: Even without solutions to the above problems, our results clearly imply that the correlation-driven MD refinement is able to generate models with a quality consistent with well-established methods given the map quality.
evidence: The Results section concludes based on the results.

claim: The accuracy and convergence of CDMD have been established and validated by applying it to a diverse set of test cases covering the most typical refinement challenges posed by modern cryo-EM.
source: We have established and validated the accuracy and convergence of CDMD by applying it to a diverse set of test cases (Figure 3-Figure 10) covering the most typical refinement challenges posed by modern cryo-EM: starting models in conformational states distant from the target map, poor starting model geometry, highly heterogeneous local map resolution, multiscale fitting where local adjustments have to be balanced by global optimization, low- or medium-resolution maps where high-resolution features have to be drawn elsewhere, or combinations thereof.
evidence: The Conclusions section summarizes the validation and references figures.

claim: The results demonstrate that all the refinement challenges can be handled by CDMD without additional backbone- and rotamer-specific restraints or manual intervention.
source: Our results demonstrate that all these challenges can be handled by CDMD without additional backbone- and rotamer-specific restraints or manual intervention.
evidence: The Conclusions section summarizes the results.

claim: CDMD has a much higher radius of convergence than current non-MD methods, which is largely independent of the map resolution and which is comparable to that of the most recent MDFF versions, namely, at least 6–7 Å in terms of the overall RMSD from the target state and at least 25 Å in terms of local deviations.
source: Yet, our method has a much higher radius of convergence than current non-MD methods, which is largely independent of the map resolution and which is comparable to that of the most recent MDFF versions (Singharoy et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018), namely, at least 6–7 Å in terms of the overall RMSD from the target state and at least 25 Å in terms of local deviations.
evidence: The Conclusions section summarizes the radius of convergence with citations.

claim: The comparisons with the alternative methods clearly illustrate the challenge of reconciling local refinement accuracy and large convergence radius, in which a proper treatment of concerted molecular motions plays a major role.
source: The comparisons with the alternative methods, however, clearly illustrate the challenge of reconciling local refinement accuracy and large convergence radius, in which a proper treatment of concerted molecular motions plays a major role.
evidence: The Conclusions section summarizes the comparison results.

claim: The CorA case demonstrates that CDMD is capable of capturing biologically relevant conformational changes, thus underlining the advantage of using the correlation-based biasing potential for low-resolution refinements.
source: Finally, the CorA case demonstrates that CDMD is capable of capturing biologically relevant conformational changes, thus underlining the advantage of using the correlation-based biasing potential for low-resolution refinements.
evidence: The Conclusions section summarizes the CorA results.

claim: The dramatic recent advances in image collection and processing have resulted in cryo-EM densities being generated at an unprecedented pace, with the refinement challenges tightly interlaced.
source: The dramatic recent advances in image collection and processing have resulted in cryo-EM densities being generated at an unprecedented pace, with the above challenges tightly interlaced.
evidence: The Conclusions section describes the state of the field.

claim: CDMD largely overcomes the shortcomings of the refinement methods available so far, namely, the poor convergence and accuracy when applied to maps with medium/low resolution (non-MD methods) or high resolution (MD-based flexible methods).
source: CDMD largely overcomes the shortcomings of the refinement methods available so far, namely, the poor convergence and accuracy when applied to maps with medium/low resolution (non-MD methods) or high resolution (MD-based flexible methods).
evidence: The Conclusions section summarizes the advantages of CDMD.

claim: Integrating well-established techniques into an optimized protocol involving a chemically accurate force field, adaptive resolution and the half-map-based validation scheme has finally allowed to overcome the shortcomings in an automated fashion.
source: Integrating well-established techniques, for example, the correlation biasing potential (Orzechowski and Tama, 2008) or simulated annealing (Brünger et al., 1987; Brunger and Adams, 2002), into an optimized protocol involving a chemically accurate force field, adaptive resolution and the half-map-based validation scheme has finally allowed to overcome these shortcomings in an automated fashion.
evidence: The Conclusions section summarizes the approach with citations.

claim: CDMD can still be used for quick (re-)refinement of close starting models against high-resolution maps or as a tool for flexible fitting of distant atomic models into low-resolution maps, which underlines its flexibility and universality.
source: We note that our method can still be used for quick (re-)refinement of close starting models against high-resolution maps (for example, Figure 6a,b) or as a tool for flexible fitting of distant atomic models into low-resolution maps (Figure 10), which underlines its flexibility and universality.
evidence: The Conclusions section describes additional applications and references figures.

claim: The implementation based on the highly scalable, GPU-accelerated GROMACS engine provides a good trade-off between refinement time and hardware cost.
source: Also, our implementation based on the highly scalable, GPU-accelerated GROMACS engine provides a good trade-off between refinement time and hardware cost (see the benchmark section in Materials and methods).
evidence: The Conclusions section describes the implementation.

claim: In combination with modern de novo chain building tools, CDMD provides a fully automated and human-bias-free framework for quantitative interpretation of modern cryo-EM data.
source: In combination with modern de novo chain building tools, it provides a fully automated and human-bias-free framework for quantitative interpretation of modern cryo-EM data.
evidence: The Conclusions section describes the potential of CDMD.

claim: The structure of the 70S ribosome in a distant conformational state (codon reading, PDB ID: 5LZC) was used as a starting model for ribosome refinement.
source: The structure of the 70S ribosome in a distant conformational state (codon reading, PDB ID: 5LZC) was used as a starting model.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the starting model.

claim: Additional Mg2+ ions were placed according to their positions in the structure of the GTPase-activated state for ribosome refinement.
source: Additional Mg2+ ions were placed according to their positions in the structure of the GTPase-activated state (Fischer et al., 2016).
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the model preparation with citation.

claim: The ribosome system was protonated, solvated, and ions were added as described previously.
source: The structure was protonated, solvated, and ions were added as described previously (Arenz et al., 2016).
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the system preparation with citation.

claim: The AMBERFF12sb force field was used for ribosome refinement.
source: The AMBERFF12sb force field was used (Lindorff-Larsen et al., 2010); further simulation parameters can be found elsewhere (Fischer et al., 2016).
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the force field with citations.

claim: The complete framework of CDMD has been embedded into the GPU-accelerated GROMACS MD suite.
source: The complete framework has been embedded into the GPU-accelerated GROMACS MD suite (Abraham et al., 2015).
evidence: The Results section describes the implementation with citation.

claim: The refinement process in CDMD is controlled by only three parameters which are varied during the MD run.
source: The refinement process is controlled by only three parameters which are varied during the MD run.
evidence: The Results section describes the refinement protocol.

claim: CHARMM36m force field was used in the CorA refinement for consistency with MDFF.
source: CHARMM36m force field (Huang et al., 2017) was used in the CorA refinement for consistency with MDFF, while CHARMM22* force field (Piana et al., 2011) was used in all other cases.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the force field choice with citations.

claim: CHARMM22* force field was used in all non-ribosomal cases except CorA.
source: CHARMM36m force field (Huang et al., 2017) was used in the CorA refinement for consistency with MDFF, while CHARMM22* force field (Piana et al., 2011) was used in all other cases.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the force field choice with citations.
